course.description: Module 00 builds the database vocabulary every later SQL module depends on: data, databases, tables, rows, columns, keys and how a query is executed.

modules.title: SQL and Database Fundamentals
modules.goal: Build the vocabulary and mental model for every later SQL module.

topics.title: What is Data?
topics.simple: Data matlab koi bhi information — naam, number, date, photo. Jaise school register me student ka naam aur marks.
topics.pro: Data is a recorded fact or value that can be stored and processed. In a database it is typed, named and organised into rows and columns.
points: Data becomes information when it is organised and interpreted.
Databases store data in typed columns, not free-form text.
A single value is a datum; many values form a dataset.

topics.title: What is a Database?
topics.simple: Database ek organised digital almari hai jisme data safely store hota hai aur baad me query karke nikal sakte hain.
topics.pro: A database is an organised collection of structured data managed by a database management system, with controlled access and durable storage.
points: It stores related data, not one flat file.
It supports concurrent readers and writers.
It enforces rules such as keys and constraints.

topics.title: Why Do We Need Databases?
topics.simple: Spreadsheet sabko bhejna messy ho jata hai; database ek jagah data rakhta hai aur sabko sahi version dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Databases centralise data, avoid duplication, enforce integrity and let many users query the same source safely.
points: One source of truth instead of many copies.
Constraints stop invalid data at write time.
Indexes make large datasets queryable.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS students FROM students;

topics.title: What is DBMS?
topics.simple: DBMS wo software hai jo database ko manage karta hai — data save, search, update aur security sambhalta hai.
topics.pro: A Database Management System is software that defines, stores, queries and administers databases; PostgreSQL and MySQL are examples.
points: It sits between the user and the files on disk.
It handles transactions, permissions and recovery.
It provides a query language such as SQL.

topics.title: What is RDBMS?
topics.simple: RDBMS ek DBMS hai jo data ko tables me rakhta hai aur tables ko keys se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A Relational Database Management System stores data in relations (tables) and enforces relationships through primary and foreign keys.
points: Tables are relations with rows and columns.
Relationships are declared, not implied by file names.
SQL is the standard query language.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;

topics.title: DBMS vs RDBMS
topics.simple: DBMS data manage karta hai; RDBMS tables aur relationships ke saath manage karta hai.
topics.pro: Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but an RDBMS adds the relational model, keys, joins and integrity constraints.
points: RDBMS enforces referential integrity.
RDBMS supports joins across related tables.
Both manage storage, access and recovery.

topics.title: What is SQL?
topics.simple: SQL wo language hai jisse hum database se baat karte hain — data lao, add karo, update karo.
topics.pro: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the declarative language used to define, query and modify relational data.
points: Declarative: you state the result you want.
Standardised, with dialect differences.
Used for DDL, DML, DQL and permissions.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Full Form of SQL
topics.simple: SQL ka full form Structured Query Language hai.
topics.pro: SQL stands for Structured Query Language; it is a standard language for relational databases, not a general-purpose programming language.
points: Structured: data lives in tables.
Query: you ask questions of the data.
Language: it has keywords, expressions and clauses.

topics.title: Why SQL Is Used
topics.simple: SQL se hum data ko filter, sort, group aur join kar sakte hain — analyst aur developer dono ise use karte hain.
topics.pro: SQL is used because it is declarative, portable across relational engines and expressive enough for filtering, aggregation, joins and analytics.
points: One language across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server.
Set-based operations scale better than row-by-row code.
Analysts, backend developers and DBAs share it.

example.sql: SELECT city, AVG(marks) AS avg_marks FROM students GROUP BY city;

topics.title: SQL vs MySQL
topics.simple: SQL language hai; MySQL ek database software hai jo SQL use karta hai.
topics.pro: SQL is the language; MySQL is an open-source RDBMS that implements it with its own dialect and storage engines.
points: SQL is a standard; MySQL is a product.
MySQL adds AUTO_INCREMENT and its own functions.
PostgreSQL and SQLite are alternative implementations.

topics.title: SQL vs PostgreSQL
topics.simple: SQL language hai; PostgreSQL ek powerful open-source database hai jo SQL ke saath advanced features deta hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL is an RDBMS known for standards compliance, rich types, transactions and extensions; SQL is the language it speaks.
points: PostgreSQL supports SERIAL/IDENTITY, JSONB and window functions.
It is stricter about types than MySQL.
The SQL language is shared; functions and types differ.

topics.title: SQL vs SQLite
topics.simple: SQL language hai; SQLite ek chhota database hai jo ek file me chalta hai — mobile apps aur browser labs me common.
topics.pro: SQLite is an embedded, serverless RDBMS stored in a single file; SQL is the query language. It is excellent for local tools and tests.
points: No server process to manage.
Typed but relaxed; fewer advanced features than PostgreSQL.
The SQL Lab in this app runs SQLite compiled to WebAssembly.

topics.title: SQL vs NoSQL
topics.simple: SQL tables me fixed columns rakhta hai; NoSQL flexible documents ya key-value me data rakhta hai.
topics.pro: SQL databases are relational and schema-first; NoSQL systems trade strict relations for flexible documents, key-value or graph models.
points: SQL excels at joins and integrity.
NoSQL often scales horizontally for flexible payloads.
Choose by access pattern, not fashion.

topics.title: What is a Database Table?
topics.simple: Table rows aur columns ka grid hai — jaise students table me har row ek student.
topics.pro: A table is a relation: a named set of columns with types, holding rows of values.
points: Columns define the shape and types.
Rows hold individual records.
Constraints on the table protect data quality.

example.output:
id | name | city | marks
1 | Aarav | Pune | 82

topics.title: What is a Row?
topics.simple: Row table ki ek line hai — ek student ka poora record.
topics.pro: A row (tuple) is one record in a table, containing one value per column.
points: Rows are unordered unless you sort.
A row can be inserted, updated or deleted.
Primary keys identify rows.

example.output:
id | name | city | marks
1 | Aarav | Pune | 82

topics.title: What is a Column?
topics.simple: Column ek vertical field hai — jaise sab students ke marks.
topics.pro: A column (attribute) is a named field with a data type shared by every row in the table.
points: Columns have types such as INT or TEXT.
Column names should be stable and descriptive.
Constraints apply per column or across columns.

topics.title: What is a Record?
topics.simple: Record ek complete entry hai — row ke barabar, jaise ek employee ki poori detail.
topics.pro: A record is one logical entry in a table, represented by a row of related field values.
points: A record spans all columns of its table.
Records are what INSERT creates and DELETE removes.
A primary key identifies each record.

example.sql: SELECT name, city FROM students WHERE id = 2;

topics.title: What is a Field?
topics.simple: Field ek single value slot hai — row aur column ka intersection.
topics.pro: A field is one column value within one row; it is the smallest addressable unit in a table.
points: A field has the column type.
NULL means the field has no value.
SELECT can return individual fields.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: What is a Database Schema?
topics.simple: Schema database ka blueprint hai — kaunsi tables, columns aur relationships hain.
topics.pro: A schema is the logical structure of a database: tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and relationships, often namespaced under a schema name.
points: DDL defines and changes the schema.
A schema is separate from the data it holds.
PostgreSQL groups objects under named schemas.

topics.title: What is a Primary Key?
topics.simple: Primary key har row ko unique pehchanta hai — jaise student ka roll number.
topics.pro: A primary key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.
points: It enforces uniqueness.
It rejects NULL values.
It is usually indexed and referenced by foreign keys.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);

topics.title: What is a Foreign Key?
topics.simple: Foreign key ek table ke column ko doosri table ke primary key se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A foreign key is a column or set of columns whose values must match a candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.
points: It prevents orphan rows.
It can cascade updates or deletes when declared.
It makes joins meaningful.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER REFERENCES students(id));

topics.title: How SQL Works
topics.simple: SQL likhne par database use parse karta hai, plan banata hai, execute karta hai aur result deta hai.
topics.pro: A SQL statement is parsed, rewritten, planned by the optimiser and executed by the engine, which returns rows or a command status.
points: Parsing checks syntax and names.
Planning chooses access paths and joins.
Execution reads and writes storage.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: How SQL Queries Are Executed
topics.simple: Database pehle samajhta hai query kya maang rahi hai, phir fastest plan chunta hai, phir data padhta hai.
topics.pro: Execution follows a logical order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — while the optimiser may reorder physical work.
points: Logical order explains aliases and aggregates.
The optimiser can push filters down.
EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan.

example.sql: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city;

topics.title: Understanding Relational Databases
topics.simple: Relational database tables ko keys se jodta hai, taaki ek hi data baar-baar na likhna pade.
topics.pro: The relational model represents data as relations and relationships through keys; normalisation reduces redundancy while joins reconstruct related facts.
points: Tables represent entities or relationships.
Keys connect rows across tables.
Joins answer questions spanning entities.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;

interview.q: What is data, and how does it differ from information?
interview.answer: Data is a raw recorded value; information is data organised and interpreted in context. A database stores data, and a query turns it into information.

interview.q: Why do we need a database?
interview.answer: To keep one durable source of truth, enforce integrity, support concurrent access and make large datasets queryable through indexes and SQL.

interview.q: What is a DBMS?
interview.answer: Software that defines, stores, queries, secures and recovers databases. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are DBMSs.

interview.q: What is an RDBMS?
interview.answer: A DBMS based on the relational model: data lives in tables, keys declare relationships and SQL is the query language.

interview.q: DBMS vs RDBMS?
interview.answer: Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but an RDBMS adds relations, keys, joins and referential integrity. A DBMS may use other models.

interview.q: What is SQL?
interview.answer: Structured Query Language, the declarative language for defining, querying and modifying relational data.

interview.q: Why is SQL declarative?
interview.answer: You describe the result you want; the optimiser chooses the execution plan. That separates intent from physical access paths.

interview.q: SQL vs MySQL?
interview.answer: SQL is the standard language; MySQL is an RDBMS product that implements it with its own dialect, storage engines and functions.

interview.q: SQL vs PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: SQL is the language; PostgreSQL is an RDBMS known for standards compliance, rich types, transactions and extensions.

interview.q: SQL vs SQLite?
interview.answer: SQL is the language; SQLite is an embedded, serverless RDBMS stored in one file, ideal for local tools and tests.

interview.q: SQL vs NoSQL?
interview.answer: SQL databases are relational and schema-first; NoSQL systems trade joins and strict integrity for flexible documents, key-value or graph models.

interview.q: What is a table?
interview.answer: A relation: a named set of typed columns holding rows. Constraints on the table protect data quality.

interview.q: What is a row?
interview.answer: One record in a table, containing one value per column. Rows are unordered unless a query sorts them.

interview.q: What is a column?
interview.answer: A named attribute with a data type shared by every row. Column names should be stable and descriptive.

interview.q: Row vs record?
interview.answer: They are effectively the same in a relational table: a record is the logical entry, a row is its physical representation.

interview.q: Column vs field?
interview.answer: A column is the whole named attribute across rows; a field is one value at a specific row-column intersection.

interview.q: What is a schema?
interview.answer: The logical structure of the database: tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and relationships, often grouped under a schema name.

interview.q: What is a primary key?
interview.answer: A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL. It is usually indexed and referenced by foreign keys.

interview.q: What is a foreign key?
interview.answer: A column or set of columns whose values must match a candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

interview.q: How is a SQL query executed?
interview.answer: The engine parses and validates it, the optimiser chooses a plan, and the executor reads or writes storage and returns rows or a command status.

labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;
labs.expected: Rows from highest to lowest marks.

labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;

labs.title: Average marks
labs.task: Return the average marks.
labs.solution: SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg_marks FROM students;

labs.title: Group by city
labs.task: Count students per city.
labs.solution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students GROUP BY city;

labs.title: Join courses
labs.task: Return student name and course title.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;
labs.expected: One row per matching student-course pair.

labs.task: Return the three highest marks.

labs.title: Between values
labs.task: Return students with marks between 60 and 90.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

labs.title: Pattern match
labs.task: Return names starting with A.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

labs.title: Null check
labs.task: Return students whose city is missing.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city IS NULL;

labs.title: Alias a column
labs.task: Return marks labelled score.
labs.solution: SELECT marks AS score FROM students;

labs.title: Calculated column
labs.task: Return marks plus 5 as boosted.
labs.solution: SELECT marks + 5 AS boosted FROM students;

labs.title: Maximum marks
labs.task: Return the highest mark.
labs.solution: SELECT MAX(marks) AS top FROM students;

labs.title: Minimum marks
labs.task: Return the lowest mark.
labs.solution: SELECT MIN(marks) AS low FROM students;

labs.title: Group with HAVING
labs.task: Return cities with more than one student.

logic.q: Why does SELECT * return columns in table order?
logic.answer: The table definition fixes column order; SELECT * expands to that order unless the query lists columns explicitly.

logic.q: Why can a primary key not be NULL?
logic.answer: A NULL cannot identify a row uniquely, so the key would fail its purpose.

logic.q: Why does a foreign key prevent orphan rows?
logic.answer: It requires each value to match a key in the referenced table, or be NULL if allowed.

logic.q: Why is SQL called declarative?
logic.answer: The query states the desired result; the optimiser chooses the execution plan.

logic.q: Why do we normalise data?
logic.answer: To reduce redundancy and avoid insert, update and delete anomalies.

logic.q: Why can two rows have the same name?
logic.answer: A name is not a key unless declared unique; only the primary key must be unique.

logic.q: Why does ORDER BY matter for LIMIT?
logic.answer: Without ORDER BY, LIMIT returns an arbitrary set; ORDER BY defines which rows are “top”.

logic.q: Why does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)?
logic.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULL values in that column.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the remaining rows are grouped and aggregated.

logic.q: Why does HAVING exist?
logic.answer: It filters groups after aggregation, which WHERE cannot do.

logic.q: Why is a schema separate from data?
logic.answer: The schema is the structure; data is the content stored within that structure.

logic.q: Why do joins need a matching key?
logic.answer: The key defines which rows from each table belong together.

logic.q: Why can an index speed up a query?
logic.answer: It lets the engine find rows without scanning the whole table.

logic.q: Why can too many indexes hurt?
logic.answer: Every write must maintain them, adding storage and latency.

logic.q: Why is SQL portable but not identical everywhere?
logic.answer: The core language is standardised, but dialects differ in types, functions and extensions.

topics.title: Introduction to SQL Editors
topics.simple: SQL editor wo jagah hai jahan query likhte hain aur Run dabate hain — pgAdmin, psql ya DBeaver.
topics.pro: An SQL editor is a client that connects to a database, lets you write statements and shows results or errors.
points: Pick one editor and learn its shortcut for Run.
The editor is only a client; the server does the work.
Keep queries formatted for review.

topics.title: Introduction to PostgreSQL
topics.simple: PostgreSQL ek powerful open-source relational database hai jo SQL ke saath advanced features deta hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL is an open-source client-server RDBMS with ACID transactions, rich types, extensions and strong SQL compliance.
points: It runs as a server on port 5432 by default.
It supports schemas, roles and extensions.
It is stricter about types than MySQL.

topics.title: PostgreSQL Installation
topics.simple: PostgreSQL ko official installer, package manager ya Docker se install kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Install PostgreSQL from the official packages, your OS package manager or a container image; the server and client tools install separately.
points: Install the server and psql/pgAdmin.
Note the port and data directory.
Start the service after install.

topics.title: PostgreSQL Database Setup
topics.simple: Install ke baad ek database banate hain aur usme tables rakhte hain.
topics.pro: After the cluster is running, create a database owned by a role, then connect to it before creating objects.
points: CREATE DATABASE needs a connection to another database.
The owner controls default privileges.
Encoding and locale are set at creation.

topics.title: pgAdmin Introduction
topics.simple: pgAdmin PostgreSQL ka graphical client hai — tables aur queries point-and-click me.
topics.pro: pgAdmin is a web/desktop client for PostgreSQL: it manages connections, databases, schemas, tables and the query tool.
points: Use the Query Tool for SQL.
The object tree shows databases and schemas.
Refresh after DDL changes.

topics.title: SQL Command Line Introduction
topics.simple: psql command line client hai — terminal se query chala sakte hain.
topics.pro: psql is PostgreSQL’s interactive terminal client; it supports meta-commands such as \l, \dt and \d.
points: Connect with psql -d database.
Meta-commands start with a backslash.
End SQL statements with a semicolon.

topics.title: Database Connection
topics.simple: Connection ka matlab client server se authenticate karke baat karta hai.
topics.pro: A connection authenticates a role to a database on a host/port and opens a session for statements.
points: Host, port, database, user and password are the core settings.
SSL protects network traffic.
Each session has its own settings.

topics.title: Creating Your First Database
topics.simple: Pehla database banane ke liye CREATE DATABASE chalao.
topics.pro: CREATE DATABASE creates a new database from a template; connect to an existing database to run it.
points: Names are case-sensitive when quoted.
The creator becomes the owner.
Template1 is the default template.

topics.title: Opening a Database
topics.simple: Database kholne ke liye \c ya client me connection choose karo.
topics.pro: Switch the current database with \c in psql or by selecting the connection in a GUI client.
points: The session’s current database changes.
Objects are resolved in the new database.
Reconnect after switching.

topics.title: Understanding Database Schemas
topics.simple: Schema database ke andar tables ka folder jaisa hai.
topics.pro: A schema is a namespace inside a database; public is the default, and search_path decides unqualified name resolution.
points: CREATE SCHEMA creates a namespace.
Qualify as schema.table.
search_path controls lookup order.

topics.title: Creating Your First Table
topics.simple: Table banane ke liye columns aur types define karo.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE declares columns, types and constraints; the table is created in the current schema.
points: Every column needs a type.
Primary keys identify rows.
NOT NULL rejects missing values.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, marks INTEGER);

topics.title: Understanding SQL Statements
topics.simple: SQL statement ek command hai — SELECT, INSERT, CREATE, etc.
topics.pro: A statement is a complete SQL command terminated by a semicolon; it may return rows or a command tag.
points: DDL changes structure.
DML changes rows.
DQL reads rows.

topics.title: Writing Your First SELECT Query
topics.simple: SELECT se data padhte hain; * sab columns deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT projects columns and rows; * expands to every column of the FROM relation.
points: List columns explicitly in production.
FROM names the table.
WHERE filters rows.

topics.title: Executing SQL Commands
topics.simple: Run dabao ya Ctrl+Enter; server query chalata hai.
topics.pro: Execution sends the statement to the server, which parses, plans, executes and returns a result or command tag.
points: Check the result tag.
Errors identify the line and token.
Transactions group writes.

topics.title: Understanding Query Results
topics.simple: Result table rows aur columns me aata hai; command tag batata hai kitne rows affect hue.
topics.pro: A result set has columns and rows; DML returns a command tag such as INSERT 0 1 or UPDATE 2.
points: SELECT returns rows.
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE return counts.
NULL is not an empty string.

topics.title: Understanding SQL Errors
topics.simple: Error message batata hai kya galat hai — table, column ya syntax.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL errors include a severity, message, detail and position; read the first error before changing the query.
points: relation does not exist means a missing table.
column does not exist means a missing name.
syntax error points at the token.

topics.title: SQL Comments
topics.simple: Comments notes hote hain jo database ignore karta hai.
topics.pro: Use -- for a line comment and /* ... */ for a block comment; comments are stripped before execution.
points: Comment why, not what.
Do not nest block comments.
Keep comments out of hot queries if noisy.

topics.title: SQL Keywords
topics.simple: Keywords reserved words hain jaise SELECT, FROM, WHERE.
topics.pro: Keywords are reserved tokens with fixed meaning; identifiers that collide must be quoted.
points: Keywords are case-insensitive.
Do not name a column order.
Quote identifiers only when needed.

topics.title: SQL Naming Conventions
topics.simple: Tables aur columns ke naam clear aur consistent rakho.
topics.pro: Use lower_snake_case for identifiers, plural table names and descriptive column names; avoid reserved words.
points: Be consistent across the schema.
Avoid quoted mixed-case names.
Name keys and constraints explicitly.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_enrollments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);

topics.title: SQL Formatting Best Practices
topics.simple: Query ko multi-line likho taaki padhna easy ho.
topics.pro: Format clauses on their own lines, indent joins and keep keywords uppercase for scanability.
points: SELECT, FROM, WHERE on separate lines.
Align JOIN conditions.
Keep one statement per semicolon.

example.sql:
SELECT name,
       marks
FROM students
WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Creating a Table with Constraints
topics.simple: Constraints data ko valid rakhte hain — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK.
topics.pro: Constraints enforce rules at write time: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY.
points: Name constraints for easier migration.
CHECK is evaluated per row.
Foreign keys need matching values.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);

topics.title: Inserting Your First Row
topics.simple: INSERT se table me naya record add hota hai.
topics.pro: INSERT adds one or more rows; RETURNING can return generated values.
points: List columns to avoid order bugs.
Strings use single quotes.
RETURNING is PostgreSQL-specific.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Meera', 91) RETURNING id;

topics.title: Reading the Query Plan
topics.simple: EXPLAIN batata hai database query kaise chalayega.
topics.pro: EXPLAIN shows the planner’s access path; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports actual timing.
points: Seq Scan means a full table scan.
Index Scan uses an index.
ANALYZE executes the statement.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Your First Database Workflow
topics.simple: Database banao, connect karo, table banao, row daalo, SELECT se check karo.
topics.pro: The first workflow is create database → connect → create table → insert → select → inspect with \d.
points: Keep DDL and seed data separate.
Verify with SELECT.
Commit when the schema is stable.

interview.q: What is PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: An open-source client-server RDBMS with ACID transactions, rich types, extensions and strong SQL compliance.

interview.q: What is the difference between a database and a schema?
interview.answer: A database is a separate catalog with its own connections; a schema is a namespace inside a database that groups tables and other objects.

interview.q: What is psql?
interview.answer: The official PostgreSQL command-line client. It supports SQL plus meta-commands such as \dt and \d.

interview.q: What is pgAdmin?
interview.answer: A graphical client for PostgreSQL that manages connections, databases, schemas, tables and queries.

interview.q: How do you connect to PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Provide host, port, database, user and password (or use a local socket); the server authenticates the role and opens a session.

interview.q: How do you create a database?
interview.answer: Run CREATE DATABASE name from a connection to an existing database; the creator becomes the owner.

interview.q: How do you switch databases in psql?
interview.answer: Use \c database_name. SQL sessions cannot switch databases with a SQL statement in PostgreSQL.

interview.q: What is the default schema?
interview.answer: public. Unqualified names resolve through search_path, which normally starts with public.

interview.q: How do you create a table?
interview.answer: CREATE TABLE name (column type constraints, ...); every column needs a type and optional constraints.

interview.q: What is a primary key?
interview.answer: A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.

interview.q: What does NOT NULL do?
interview.answer: It rejects inserts or updates that leave the column without a value.

interview.q: What does UNIQUE do?
interview.answer: It rejects duplicate non-NULL values in the column or column set.

interview.q: What does CHECK do?
interview.answer: It rejects rows where the boolean expression is false or NULL.

interview.q: What is a foreign key?
interview.answer: A column or set of columns whose values must match a candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

interview.q: How do you insert a row?
interview.answer: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values); use RETURNING to get generated values.

interview.q: What does SELECT * do?
interview.answer: It returns every column of the relation; listing columns explicitly is safer in production.

interview.q: What does EXPLAIN do?
interview.answer: It shows the planner’s chosen access path without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs it.

interview.q: What is a command tag?
interview.answer: The status line returned by DML/DDL, such as INSERT 0 1 or UPDATE 2, reporting affected rows.

interview.q: How do you comment SQL?
interview.answer: Use -- for a line comment and /* ... */ for a block comment.

interview.q: What is a good first workflow?
interview.answer: Create the database, connect, create tables, insert seed rows, select to verify, then inspect with \d.

logic.q: Why does CREATE DATABASE fail inside a transaction?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL does not allow CREATE DATABASE in a transaction block; run it outside a transaction.

logic.q: Why does an unquoted name fold to lowercase?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase; quoted names preserve case.

logic.q: Why does SELECT * break after a schema change?
logic.answer: It returns the new column set, which can break consumers that expected a fixed shape.

logic.q: Why does a foreign key reject an insert?
logic.answer: The referenced key does not exist in the parent table.

logic.q: Why does a CHECK constraint reject NULL?
logic.answer: A CHECK passes only when the expression is true; NULL is not true.

logic.q: Why does ORDER BY matter for LIMIT?
logic.answer: Without ORDER BY, LIMIT returns an arbitrary set of rows.

logic.q: Why does COUNT(column) differ from COUNT(*)?
logic.answer: COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the remaining rows are grouped.

logic.q: Why is HAVING needed?
logic.answer: It filters groups after aggregation, which WHERE cannot do.

logic.q: Why use RETURNING on INSERT?
logic.answer: It returns generated values such as ids in the same statement.

logic.q: Why is EXPLAIN useful?
logic.answer: It shows the access path and helps spot sequential scans.

logic.q: Why is a schema useful?
logic.answer: It namespaces objects and lets search_path resolve unqualified names.

logic.q: Why does a transaction rollback?
logic.answer: An error aborts the transaction until ROLLBACK or COMMIT after a successful statement.

logic.q: Why avoid reserved words as identifiers?
logic.answer: They require quoting and make queries harder to read.

logic.q: Why keep DDL and seed data separate?
logic.answer: Schema changes and data can be reviewed, rerun and rolled back independently.

modules.title: SQL Data Types
modules.goal: Choose correct PostgreSQL types and convert values safely.

topics.title: What Are SQL Data Types?
topics.simple: Data type batata hai ki column me kis tarah ki value store hogi — number, text, date ya true/false.
topics.pro: A data type defines the domain of values a column can hold, the storage representation and the operations PostgreSQL allows on it.
points: Every column needs a type.
The type controls valid values and operators.
PostgreSQL checks types when rows are written.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE demo (id INTEGER, name TEXT);

topics.title: Why Data Types Matter
topics.simple: Sahi type se data saaf rehta hai, storage bachta hai aur galat value galti se save nahi hoti.
topics.pro: Types enforce correctness, choose the right storage size and let the planner use the right operators and indexes.
points: A wrong type can reject valid data or accept invalid data.
Numeric types keep arithmetic exact or approximate by design.
Text types differ in length rules and padding.

topics.title: The Integer Family
topics.simple: Integer family me SMALLINT, INTEGER aur BIGINT aate hain — teeno whole numbers hain, bas range alag hai.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL has three integer types: smallint (2 bytes), integer (4 bytes) and bigint (8 bytes); all are exact whole numbers with different ranges.
points: SMALLINT: -32768 to 32767.
INTEGER: about -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion.
BIGINT: about -9.2 quintillion to 9.2 quintillion.

topics.title: SMALLINT
topics.simple: SMALLINT chhote whole numbers ke liye 2 bytes leta hai; range se bahar value error deti hai.
topics.pro: SMALLINT is a 2-byte signed integer with a range of -32768 to 32767, useful for small counts and compact rows.
points: Use it only when the range is guaranteed.
A value of 32768 fails.
It is exact, unlike floating-point types.

topics.title: INTEGER
topics.simple: INTEGER sabse common whole-number type hai — 4 bytes aur lagbhag 2.1 billion tak.
topics.pro: INTEGER (INT) is a 4-byte signed integer from -2147483648 to 2147483647 and is the default choice for ids and counts.
points: It is exact.
It is the usual primary-key type.
Overflow raises an error rather than wrapping.

topics.title: BIGINT
topics.simple: BIGINT 8 bytes leta hai aur bahut bade whole numbers ke liye hai.
topics.pro: BIGINT is an 8-byte signed integer from -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807, used for large counters and external ids.
points: It is exact.
It costs twice the storage of INTEGER.
Use it for values that can outgrow 2.1 billion.

topics.title: DECIMAL and NUMERIC
topics.simple: DECIMAL aur NUMERIC exact decimal numbers hain — paise jaise values ke liye.
topics.pro: DECIMAL is an alias for NUMERIC in PostgreSQL; both store exact numbers with a fixed precision and scale.
points: Use NUMERIC for money and exact measurements.
DECIMAL and NUMERIC behave the same.
They are slower than binary floating point.

topics.title: NUMERIC Precision and Scale
topics.simple: NUMERIC(p,s) me p total digits aur s decimal ke baad ke digits hote hain.
topics.pro: NUMERIC(precision, scale) allows precision total digits, with scale digits after the decimal point; NUMERIC(5,2) stores up to 999.99.
points: Precision counts all digits, not just the integer part.
Scale is the number of fractional digits.
A value that does not fit raises numeric field overflow.

topics.title: REAL
topics.simple: REAL 4-byte approximate floating-point number hai — speed acchi, exactness nahi.
topics.pro: REAL is a 4-byte single-precision floating-point type with about 6 significant digits; it is approximate, not exact.
points: Use it for scientific measurements, not money.
Equality comparisons can surprise you.
It stores a binary approximation.

topics.title: DOUBLE PRECISION
topics.simple: DOUBLE PRECISION 8-byte floating-point number hai — REAL se zyada precision, phir bhi approximate.
topics.pro: DOUBLE PRECISION is an 8-byte double-precision floating-point type with about 15 significant digits; it is approximate.
points: It is not exact for decimal fractions.
Use NUMERIC when exactness matters.
It is the usual choice for scientific data.

topics.title: CHAR
topics.simple: CHAR(n) fixed-length text hai — chhoti value ko spaces se pad karta hai.
topics.pro: CHAR(n) is blank-padded fixed-length character data; PostgreSQL physically pads to n characters and ignores trailing spaces in comparisons.
points: CHAR(5) with ab is physically padded to 5 characters.
LENGTH() strips trailing spaces, so it returns 2; OCTET_LENGTH returns 5.
It is rarely the best choice in PostgreSQL.

topics.title: VARCHAR
topics.simple: VARCHAR(n) variable-length text hai, maximum n characters; chhoti value pad nahi hoti.
topics.pro: VARCHAR(n) stores variable-length text with a maximum of n characters and does not blank-pad shorter values.
points: The limit is characters, not bytes.
A longer value raises an error on insert.
VARCHAR without n is allowed but behaves like TEXT.

topics.title: TEXT
topics.simple: TEXT variable-length text hai jiski practical limit lagbhag 1 GB hai.
topics.pro: TEXT stores variable-length strings up to about 1 GB and has no declared length limit; in PostgreSQL it is not slower than VARCHAR.
points: PostgreSQL stores TEXT, VARCHAR and CHAR similarly.
Use TEXT when no business limit exists.
Add CHECK constraints if a limit is a real rule.

topics.title: BOOLEAN
topics.simple: BOOLEAN sirf true, false ya NULL rakhta hai.
topics.pro: BOOLEAN is a 1-byte type with three values: true, false and NULL; input accepts true/false, yes/no, on/off and 1/0.
points: Do not use text for flags.
NULL means unknown, not false.
It reads clearly in queries.

topics.title: DATE
topics.simple: DATE sirf calendar date rakhta hai — saal, mahina, din; time nahi.
topics.pro: DATE stores a calendar date without a time of day, using 4 bytes; it accepts ISO input such as 2026-01-15.
points: It has no time component.
Use it for birthdays and joining dates.
Date arithmetic works with intervals.

topics.title: TIME
topics.simple: TIME din ka time rakhta hai — ghante, minute, second; date nahi.
topics.pro: TIME stores a time of day without a date, using 8 bytes; TIME WITH TIME ZONE also exists but is rarely appropriate.
points: It has no date component.
Use it for opening hours and schedules.
Combine it with DATE when both are needed.

topics.title: TIMESTAMP
topics.simple: TIMESTAMP date aur time dono rakhta hai, lekin time zone nahi.
topics.pro: TIMESTAMP (without time zone) stores a date and time with no zone information; it records what the clock said, not an instant.
points: It is wall-clock time.
It does not convert between zones.
Use it for local schedules with a known zone.

topics.title: TIMESTAMPTZ
topics.simple: TIMESTAMPTZ actual instant store karta hai aur session ke time zone me dikhata hai.
topics.pro: TIMESTAMPTZ stores an absolute instant internally in UTC and displays it in the session time zone; it is the right type for events across zones.
points: It stores an instant, not a wall clock.
The displayed offset depends on the session.
Use it for created_at and paid_at.

topics.title: UUID
topics.simple: UUID 16-byte unique identifier hai — random ya generated, integer id ke alternative ke roop me.
topics.pro: UUID is a 16-byte universally unique identifier type; PostgreSQL can generate one with gen_random_uuid() and compare it efficiently.
points: It avoids guessing sequential ids.
It is larger than an integer.
It is not automatically indexed.

topics.title: Choosing the Right Type
topics.simple: Type choose karte waqt value ki nature, range, exactness aur storage dekho.
topics.pro: Choose by domain: exact whole numbers use integers, exact decimals use NUMERIC, timestamps use TIMESTAMPTZ, flags use BOOLEAN and unbounded text uses TEXT.
points: Prefer the narrowest type that cannot overflow.
Use NUMERIC for money.
Use TIMESTAMPTZ for real-world events.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE payments (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, amount NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL, paid_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now());

topics.title: Type Compatibility
topics.simple: Har type ko har doosre type ke saath mix nahi kar sakte; compatible types hi arithmetic ya comparison karte hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL resolves operators through type categories and casts; numeric types mix with numeric types, but text and integer do not compare without an explicit cast.
points: Integer and numeric mix in arithmetic.
Text and integer are not implicitly equal.
Unknown string literals are coerced to the other operand type.

topics.title: Implicit Conversion
topics.simple: Implicit conversion database khud karta hai, lekin PostgreSQL me yeh limited aur predictable hai.
topics.pro: An implicit cast is applied automatically by PostgreSQL when an operator or assignment needs a compatible type; PostgreSQL avoids risky implicit casts such as text to integer.
points: Assignment casts apply on INSERT.
Unknown literals take the column type.
Do not rely on implicit text-to-number conversion.

topics.title: Explicit Conversion and CAST
topics.simple: Explicit conversion me aap khud CAST ya :: se type badalte hain.
topics.pro: CAST(value AS type) and the PostgreSQL shorthand value::type perform an explicit conversion and make the intent visible in the query.
points: CAST is standard SQL.
:: is shorter PostgreSQL syntax.
An impossible conversion raises an error.

topics.title: Common Data Type Errors
topics.simple: Galat type ya galat value se invalid input, overflow ya value-too-long error aata hai.
topics.pro: Common failures are invalid input syntax, numeric field overflow, value too long for type character varying(n) and cannot cast type X to Y.
points: Read the first error and the supplied value.
Check precision and length before inserting.
Use explicit casts when the source is text.

example.output: ERROR: invalid input syntax for type integer: "abc"

topics.title: Designing an Employees Table
topics.simple: Ab sab types ko milakar ek real employees table design karte hain.
topics.pro: A production-shaped employees table uses an identity BIGINT key, bounded text, exact NUMERIC salary, BOOLEAN flags and DATE/TIMESTAMPTZ columns.
points: Use identity instead of legacy SERIAL for new tables.
Constrain text lengths that are real business rules.
Store timestamps with time zone.

example.sql:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  salary NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (salary >= 0),
  active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  joined_on DATE NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

learn.why: BOOLEAN is three-valued: true, false and unknown (NULL).

learn.q: What does DATE store?
options: A date and a time zone
learn.why: DATE has no time-of-day component.

learn.q: What does TIME store?
options: A time of day without a date
learn.answer: A time of day without a date
learn.why: TIME stores hours, minutes and seconds without a date.

learn.q: What does TIMESTAMP without time zone store?
options: A date and wall-clock time with no zone
learn.answer: A date and wall-clock time with no zone
learn.why: TIMESTAMP records what the clock said, without zone conversion.

learn.q: What does TIMESTAMPTZ store internally?
learn.why: TIMESTAMPTZ stores an instant and displays it in the session zone.

learn.q: How many bytes does UUID use?
learn.why: UUID is a 16-byte binary value; the text form is 36 characters.

learn.q: Which type is best for money?
learn.why: NUMERIC is exact; floating-point types can lose cents.

learn.q: Which is PostgreSQL explicit cast syntax?
learn.why: PostgreSQL supports the :: shorthand; CAST(value AS type) is standard SQL.

learn.q: What does CAST(42.4 AS INTEGER) return?
learn.why: PostgreSQL rounds numeric to the nearest integer when casting.

interview.q: What is a data type?
interview.answer: A definition of the values a column can hold, how they are stored and which operators are valid.

interview.q: Why does choosing the right data type matter?
interview.answer: It enforces correctness, uses appropriate storage, enables the right operators and keeps indexes efficient.

interview.q: What are the three PostgreSQL integer types?
interview.answer: SMALLINT (2 bytes), INTEGER (4 bytes) and BIGINT (8 bytes), all exact signed whole numbers with different ranges.

interview.q: When would you use BIGINT instead of INTEGER?
interview.answer: When values can exceed about 2.1 billion, such as large counters, external ids or high-volume event tables.

interview.q: What is the difference between NUMERIC and REAL?
interview.answer: NUMERIC is exact with a fixed precision and scale; REAL is an approximate 4-byte binary floating-point type.

interview.q: Are DECIMAL and NUMERIC different in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: No. DECIMAL is an alias for NUMERIC and they behave identically.

interview.q: Explain NUMERIC(precision, scale).
interview.answer: Precision is the total number of significant digits; scale is the number of digits after the decimal point. NUMERIC(5,2) allows up to 999.99.

interview.q: What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR?
interview.answer: CHAR(n) is blank-padded to exactly n characters; VARCHAR(n) is variable-length with a maximum of n and no padding.

interview.q: Is VARCHAR faster than TEXT in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: No. PostgreSQL stores all three character types similarly; choose by semantics, not by a performance myth.

interview.q: When should you use CHAR?
interview.answer: Almost never for new schemas. Use it only for genuinely fixed-width codes where blank padding is acceptable.

interview.q: How does BOOLEAN handle NULL?
interview.answer: NULL means unknown, not false. Three-valued logic applies in comparisons and CHECK constraints.

interview.q: What is the difference between DATE and TIMESTAMP?
interview.answer: DATE stores only a calendar date; TIMESTAMP stores a date and wall-clock time without a zone.

interview.q: What is the difference between TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ?
interview.answer: TIMESTAMP stores a wall-clock value with no zone; TIMESTAMPTZ stores an absolute instant in UTC and displays it in the session zone.

interview.q: When should you use TIMESTAMPTZ?
interview.answer: For real-world events such as created_at, paid_at or login time, especially when users or servers span time zones.

interview.q: What are the trade-offs of UUID keys?
interview.answer: They are globally unique and hard to guess, but larger than integers and can hurt index locality when random.

interview.q: What is the difference between SERIAL and IDENTITY?
interview.answer: SERIAL is a legacy pseudo-type that creates a sequence and default; GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is standard SQL and the preferred choice for new tables.

interview.q: What is an implicit conversion?
interview.answer: A cast PostgreSQL applies automatically when an operator or assignment requires a compatible type. PostgreSQL keeps these conservative.

interview.q: What is an explicit conversion?
interview.answer: A cast you write with CAST(value AS type) or value::type, making the intent and possible failure visible.

interview.q: Why does text = integer fail in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: There is no implicit cast between text and integer for equality; cast one side explicitly, such as id::text = code.

interview.q: What are common data type errors?
interview.answer: Invalid input syntax, numeric field overflow, value too long for varchar(n), and cannot cast type X to Y.

logic.q: Why is NUMERIC preferred over REAL for money?
logic.answer: NUMERIC is exact; REAL stores a binary approximation that can lose cents.

logic.q: Why should names generally not use CHAR?
logic.answer: CHAR blank-pads to a fixed width, which surprises comparisons and wastes space for variable-length names.

logic.q: Why is TIMESTAMPTZ better than TIMESTAMP for created_at?
logic.answer: It stores an absolute instant, so the same event reads correctly in every time zone.

logic.q: Why can a random UUID hurt index locality?
logic.answer: Random keys insert across the B-tree instead of appending, causing more page splits than sequential integers.

logic.q: Why does 7 / 2 return 3?
logic.answer: Both operands are integers, so PostgreSQL performs integer division and truncates the fraction.

logic.q: How do you get 3.5 from 7 and 2?
logic.answer: Cast at least one operand to NUMERIC, for example 7::NUMERIC / 2.

logic.q: Why does NUMERIC(5,2) reject 1234.56?
logic.answer: The value needs four integer digits plus two fractional digits, exceeding the five total digits allowed.

logic.q: Why does VARCHAR(5) reject a six-character value?
logic.answer: The declared maximum is five characters; PostgreSQL raises value too long for type character varying(5).

logic.q: Why does CHAR(5) compare equal to a shorter value?
logic.answer: CHAR is blank-padded, and PostgreSQL ignores trailing spaces in char comparisons.

logic.q: Why is TEXT not a slow choice in PostgreSQL?
logic.answer: TEXT, VARCHAR and CHAR share a similar variable-length representation; the type name does not add a performance penalty.

logic.q: Why does text = integer fail?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL has no implicit text-to-integer equality cast, so one side must be cast explicitly.

logic.q: Why prefer IDENTITY over SERIAL for new tables?
logic.answer: IDENTITY is standard SQL, keeps sequence ownership explicit and avoids the legacy pseudo-type quirks of SERIAL.

logic.q: Why store real-world event times in UTC?
logic.answer: UTC is an unambiguous instant; display conversion happens per session or application time zone.

logic.q: Why avoid the MONEY type for new schemas?
logic.answer: MONEY depends on locale settings and has limited precision; NUMERIC is portable and explicit.

logic.q: Why does CAST(42.6 AS INTEGER) return 43?
logic.answer: Casting numeric to integer rounds to the nearest whole number instead of truncating.

modules.title: SQL Commands and Categories
modules.goal: Classify SQL commands and use the right one safely.

topics.title: What Are SQL Commands?
topics.simple: SQL command ek instruction hai jo database ko kuch karne bolta hai — data laana, badalna, structure banana ya permission dena.
topics.pro: An SQL command is a statement the server parses and executes; commands are grouped by intent such as defining structure, manipulating rows, querying, controlling access or managing transactions.
points: A statement ends with a semicolon.
The command category describes its job, not its difficulty.
PostgreSQL also has utility commands such as EXPLAIN and VACUUM.

topics.title: DDL — Data Definition Language
topics.simple: DDL structure define karta hai — table, schema, index, view.
topics.pro: DDL defines and changes database objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, COMMENT and RENAME.
points: DDL changes the schema, not individual row values.
In PostgreSQL, most DDL is transactional.
DDL takes locks that can block concurrent work.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: DML — Data Manipulation Language
topics.simple: DML rows ke data ko badalta hai — insert, update, delete.
topics.pro: DML changes row data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE; it is transactional and can be filtered with WHERE.
points: DML works inside the table structure.
Every DML statement can be rolled back in PostgreSQL.
RETURNING exposes changed rows.

topics.title: DQL — Data Query Language
topics.simple: DQL data padhne ke liye hai — mainly SELECT.
topics.pro: DQL reads data without changing it; SELECT is the core DQL statement, including joins, aggregates and window functions.
points: DQL does not modify rows.
Some curricula fold DQL into DML; both names describe SELECT.
SELECT can call functions and use CTEs.

topics.title: DCL — Data Control Language
topics.simple: DCL permissions deta aur hataata hai — GRANT aur REVOKE.
topics.pro: DCL manages privileges and access: GRANT and REVOKE on databases, schemas, tables, sequences and functions.
points: Roles are the subjects of privileges.
Least privilege keeps production safe.
GRANT and REVOKE are transactional in PostgreSQL.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON students TO analyst;

topics.title: TCL — Transaction Control Language
topics.simple: TCL transaction ko control karta hai — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
topics.pro: TCL groups statements into atomic units: BEGIN/START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.
points: A transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
An error aborts the transaction until rollback.
SAVEPOINT allows partial rollback.

topics.title: CREATE
topics.simple: CREATE naya object banata hai — database, schema, table, view, index, role.
topics.pro: CREATE defines a new database object with its columns, constraints, options and owner.
points: CREATE TABLE needs column names and types.
CREATE is DDL.
Use IF NOT EXISTS when re-running scripts.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: ALTER
topics.simple: ALTER existing object ki definition badalta hai — column add, type change, constraint add.
topics.pro: ALTER modifies an existing object; ALTER TABLE can add/drop columns, change types, rename objects and manage constraints.
points: ALTER is DDL.
Some changes rewrite the table and take time.
Use USING when a type change needs an explicit cast.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;

topics.title: DROP
topics.simple: DROP object ko poora hata deta hai — structure, data aur uske dependents.
topics.pro: DROP removes an object and its data; DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW, DROP INDEX, DROP SCHEMA and DROP DATABASE are DDL.
points: DROP is destructive and usually irreversible.
Use IF EXISTS for idempotent scripts.
CASCADE also drops dependent objects; use it deliberately.

topics.title: TRUNCATE
topics.simple: TRUNCATE table ke saare rows jaldi hata deta hai, table structure rehta hai.
topics.pro: TRUNCATE removes every row from a table in one operation, resets storage, keeps the table and is transactional in PostgreSQL.
points: TRUNCATE has no WHERE clause.
RESTART IDENTITY resets sequences.
It does not fire row-level DELETE triggers.

example.sql: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

topics.title: SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT data padhta hai — columns, rows aur expressions.
topics.pro: SELECT projects columns and filters rows; it is DQL and the most common read command.
points: SELECT does not change stored rows.
Use explicit columns in production.
ORDER BY and LIMIT shape the result.

example.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: INSERT
topics.simple: INSERT table me naye rows add karta hai.
topics.pro: INSERT adds one or more rows; RETURNING returns generated values such as identity ids.
points: List columns explicitly.
INSERT ... SELECT copies rows from a query.
A failed INSERT does not add a partial row.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (id, name) VALUES (2, 'Meera') RETURNING id;

topics.title: UPDATE
topics.simple: UPDATE existing rows ke values badalta hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE changes column values for rows matched by WHERE; without WHERE every row is updated.
points: Always test the WHERE with SELECT first.
RETURNING shows what changed.
An UPDATE can fire row-level triggers.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav Sharma' WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name;

topics.title: DELETE
topics.simple: DELETE selected rows ko hataata hai, structure rehta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE removes rows matched by WHERE; without WHERE every row is deleted.
points: DELETE can be filtered and rolled back.
It fires row-level DELETE triggers.
It does not reset identity sequences.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 2 RETURNING id;

topics.title: GRANT
topics.simple: GRANT role ko permission deta hai — read, write, execute.
topics.pro: GRANT gives privileges on objects to roles; privileges include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, USAGE and EXECUTE.
points: Grant the minimum needed.
Schema USAGE is often required before table access.
GRANT is DCL.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON students TO analyst;

topics.title: REVOKE
topics.simple: REVOKE di hui permission wapas leta hai.
topics.pro: REVOKE removes privileges from roles; CASCADE also revokes dependent grants, RESTRICT refuses if dependents exist.
points: REVOKE ALL removes every privilege on the object.
Test the role after revoking.
REVOKE is DCL.

example.sql: REVOKE INSERT ON students FROM analyst;

topics.title: COMMIT
topics.simple: COMMIT transaction ke changes ko permanent karta hai.
topics.pro: COMMIT ends the transaction and makes its changes durable and visible to other sessions.
points: Commit only when the unit is complete.
COMMIT releases locks.
An aborted transaction cannot be committed.

topics.title: ROLLBACK
topics.simple: ROLLBACK transaction ke uncommitted changes ko undo karta hai.
topics.pro: ROLLBACK aborts the current transaction and discards its changes; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work after that savepoint.
points: Rollback is your safety net.
An error puts the transaction in a failed state.
DROP DATABASE cannot be rolled back because it cannot run in a transaction.

topics.title: Command Differences and Classification
topics.simple: Har command ka category alag hai; same result alag commands se aa sakta hai, par risk aur locking alag hoti hai.
topics.pro: Classify commands by intent: DDL changes structure, DML changes rows, DQL reads, DCL controls access and TCL controls transactions; some commands are utility commands outside the five groups.
points: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP differ in scope and recovery.
TRUNCATE is commonly grouped with DDL but is transactional in PostgreSQL.
SELECT is DQL even though some teams call it DML.

example.output:
DDL | CREATE TABLE
DML | INSERT
DQL | SELECT

topics.title: Practical Command Classification
topics.simple: Practice me command dekho aur bolo — structure, data, read, permission ya transaction.
topics.pro: In practice, read the verb and the target: CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE are DDL, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE are DML, SELECT is DQL, GRANT/REVOKE are DCL and BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT are TCL.
points: EXPLAIN, VACUUM, ANALYZE and COPY are utility commands.
MERGE is DML in PostgreSQL 15+.
The category guides review, permissions and rollback planning.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;
example.output: Utility command: shows the query plan.

learn.q: Which category does CREATE TABLE belong to?
learn.why: CREATE defines schema objects, which is DDL.

learn.q: Which category does INSERT belong to?
learn.why: INSERT changes row data, which is DML.

learn.q: Which category does SELECT belong to?
learn.why: SELECT reads data; many curricula name that DQL.

learn.q: Which category does GRANT belong to?
learn.why: GRANT controls privileges, which is DCL.

learn.q: Which category does COMMIT belong to?
learn.why: COMMIT ends a transaction, which is TCL.

learn.q: Which command removes all rows but keeps the table?
learn.why: TRUNCATE removes rows and keeps the table definition.

learn.q: Which command removes the table structure and its data?
learn.why: DROP removes the object itself.

learn.q: Which command adds a column to an existing table?
learn.why: ALTER changes an existing table definition.

learn.q: Which command can use a WHERE clause?
learn.why: DELETE supports WHERE; TRUNCATE does not.

learn.q: Which command fires row-level DELETE triggers?
learn.why: DELETE removes rows one by one and fires row triggers; TRUNCATE does not.

learn.q: Which command gives a role read access?
learn.why: GRANT adds a privilege to a role.

learn.q: Which command removes a privilege?
learn.why: REVOKE takes a privilege away.

learn.q: Which command makes transaction changes durable?
learn.why: COMMIT ends the transaction and persists its changes.

learn.q: Which command undoes uncommitted changes?
learn.why: ROLLBACK aborts the transaction.

learn.q: Which command starts a transaction in PostgreSQL?
learn.why: BEGIN or START TRANSACTION starts a transaction.

learn.q: Which command is DDL?
learn.why: TRUNCATE is commonly grouped with DDL because it resets table storage.

learn.q: Which command is DML?
learn.why: MERGE inserts, updates or deletes rows, so it is DML.

learn.q: Which command is a utility command, not DML?
learn.why: EXPLAIN reports a plan and does not change rows.

learn.q: Which statement is true about TRUNCATE in PostgreSQL?
learn.why: PostgreSQL TRUNCATE is transactional, unlike MySQL where it causes an implicit commit.

learn.q: What happens to an UPDATE without WHERE?
options: Only the first row is updated
learn.why: Without a WHERE predicate, UPDATE targets the whole table.

interview.q: What are the five common SQL command categories?
interview.answer: DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL. Utility commands such as EXPLAIN and VACUUM sit outside those five.

interview.q: What is DDL?
interview.answer: Data Definition Language defines and changes schema objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, COMMENT and RENAME.

interview.q: What is DML?
interview.answer: Data Manipulation Language changes row data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.

interview.q: Is SELECT DML or DQL?
interview.answer: It is DQL in the five-category model. Some teams call it DML because it operates on data, but it does not modify rows.

interview.q: What is DCL?
interview.answer: Data Control Language manages privileges: GRANT and REVOKE.

interview.q: What is TCL?
interview.answer: Transaction Control Language manages transactions: BEGIN/START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.

interview.q: What is the difference between CREATE and ALTER?
interview.answer: CREATE makes a new object; ALTER changes an existing object definition.

interview.q: What is the difference between DROP and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DROP removes the object and its data; TRUNCATE removes every row but keeps the table definition.

interview.q: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DELETE can filter with WHERE, fires row triggers and is row-by-row; TRUNCATE removes all rows in one operation, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and resets storage.

interview.q: Is TRUNCATE transactional in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Yes. It can be rolled back in PostgreSQL. In MySQL, TRUNCATE causes an implicit commit.

interview.q: Does DELETE reset an identity sequence?
interview.answer: No. DELETE leaves the sequence alone; TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY resets it.

interview.q: Why is UPDATE without WHERE dangerous?
interview.answer: It updates every row in the table. Test the predicate with SELECT and use a transaction.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: It returns rows affected by INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in the same statement, including generated ids.

interview.q: What is the difference between GRANT and REVOKE?
interview.answer: GRANT gives privileges to a role; REVOKE removes them.

interview.q: Why is schema USAGE needed before table access?
interview.answer: Object names live in a schema. A role needs USAGE on the schema and a privilege on the table to query it.

interview.q: What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?
interview.answer: COMMIT makes transaction changes durable; ROLLBACK discards them.

interview.q: What is a SAVEPOINT?
interview.answer: A named point inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work after it.

interview.q: Can CREATE DATABASE run inside a transaction?
interview.answer: No. PostgreSQL rejects CREATE DATABASE and DROP DATABASE inside a transaction block.

interview.q: Which commands are utility commands?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN, VACUUM, ANALYZE and COPY are utility commands; they are not DDL, DML, DQL, DCL or TCL.

interview.q: Is MERGE DML?
interview.answer: Yes. PostgreSQL 15+ supports MERGE, which inserts, updates or deletes rows in one statement.

logic.q: Why is TRUNCATE faster than DELETE for all rows?
logic.answer: TRUNCATE removes the table storage in one operation instead of scanning and deleting rows one by one.

logic.q: Why is DELETE often safer than TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: DELETE supports WHERE, fires row triggers and can be rolled back row by row; TRUNCATE always removes every row.

logic.q: Why is DROP more dangerous than TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: DROP removes the table definition, data, indexes and constraints; TRUNCATE keeps the table.

logic.q: Why can PostgreSQL roll back TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL implements TRUNCATE transactionally, so it can be undone before COMMIT.

logic.q: Why does MySQL commit after TRUNCATE?
logic.answer: MySQL performs an implicit commit for TRUNCATE, so it cannot be rolled back there.

logic.q: Why does TRUNCATE not fire row-level DELETE triggers?
logic.answer: It does not delete rows one by one; PostgreSQL offers statement-level TRUNCATE triggers instead.

logic.q: Why should GRANT follow least privilege?
logic.answer: A role should get only the privileges its job needs, limiting the damage of a mistake or a compromised account.

logic.q: Why is schema USAGE required?
logic.answer: The role must be able to resolve names in the schema before table privileges can be used.

logic.q: Why is UPDATE without WHERE a production incident?
logic.answer: It changes every row in the table, and a mistaken predicate can corrupt the whole dataset.

logic.q: Why test a WHERE with SELECT before DELETE?
logic.answer: The SELECT shows exactly which rows will be removed before the destructive statement runs.

logic.q: Why is SELECT classified as DQL?
logic.answer: It reads rows without modifying them; DQL exists to separate reading from DML.

logic.q: Why is CREATE TABLE AS classified as DDL?
logic.answer: It creates a new table object, even though its source is a query.

logic.q: Why is EXPLAIN not DML?
logic.answer: It reports the planner’s access path and does not change rows.

logic.q: Why is MERGE DML?
logic.answer: MERGE can insert, update or delete rows based on a source relation.

logic.q: Why can DROP DATABASE not be rolled back?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL does not allow DROP DATABASE inside a transaction block.

topics.title: CREATE DATABASE
topics.simple: CREATE DATABASE ek naya database banata hai — apne tables, schemas aur users ke saath.
topics.pro: CREATE DATABASE creates a new database catalog from a template; it must run outside a transaction block and requires the CREATEDB privilege or superuser.
points: The creator becomes the owner unless OWNER is given.
It clones template1 by default.
You cannot run it inside BEGIN ... COMMIT.

topics.title: Database Naming Rules
topics.simple: Database ka naam clear aur consistent rakho; unquoted naam lowercase ban jaate hain.
topics.pro: Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase, are limited to 63 bytes and should avoid reserved words; quoted mixed-case names must be quoted forever.
points: Use lower_snake_case.
Avoid spaces and reserved words.
Names are limited to 63 bytes.

example.output: Creates schooldb (unquoted names fold to lowercase).

topics.title: CREATE DATABASE Options
topics.simple: Database banate waqt owner, template aur encoding choose kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: CREATE DATABASE accepts OWNER, TEMPLATE, ENCODING, locale, CONNECTION LIMIT and IS_TEMPLATE options; template0 is the safe base when changing encoding or locale.
points: template1 carries local customizations.
template0 is pristine.
Set the owner explicitly in shared environments.

example.sql: CREATE DATABASE school OWNER analyst TEMPLATE template0 ENCODING 'UTF8';

topics.title: CREATE TABLE
topics.simple: CREATE TABLE columns, types aur rules ke saath naya table banata hai.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE defines a relation with ordered columns, types and constraints; it is DDL and takes a lock on the new table name.
points: Every column needs a type.
Constraints enforce rules at write time.
The table is created in the current schema.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Table Structure
topics.simple: Table structure ka matlab columns, unke types aur constraints ka plan.
topics.pro: A table structure is its ordered column list, data types, defaults, nullability and constraints; psql shows it with \d.
points: Column order is part of the definition.
Constraints protect data quality.
Indexes are separate objects.

example.output:
Table "public.students"
 id   | integer | not null
 name | text    | not null

topics.title: Defining Columns
topics.simple: Har column ka naam, type aur optional default ya constraint likho.
topics.pro: A column definition is `name type [constraints]`; defaults and constraints are evaluated when rows are written.
points: Name columns by meaning.
Put NOT NULL on required fields.
Defaults apply when the column is omitted.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL, credits SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 3);

topics.title: Defining Data Types
topics.simple: Column ke liye sahi type choose karo — number, text, date ya boolean.
topics.pro: Choose types by domain: integers for counts, NUMERIC for exact decimals, TEXT/VARCHAR for strings, BOOLEAN for flags and TIMESTAMPTZ for instants.
points: The type controls valid values and storage.
Use NUMERIC for money.
Use TIMESTAMPTZ for real-world events.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE marks (student_id INTEGER, score NUMERIC(5,2) CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100));

topics.title: Column Constraints
topics.simple: Constraints rules hain — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, PRIMARY KEY, REFERENCES.
topics.pro: Column constraints enforce nullability, uniqueness, value ranges, defaults and referential integrity; named constraints are easier to migrate later.
points: NOT NULL rejects missing values.
UNIQUE rejects duplicates.
CHECK rejects false predicates.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE);

topics.title: Creating Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Ek table me jitne columns chahiye, comma se likho.
topics.pro: A table can declare many columns in one CREATE TABLE; order is preserved and each column has its own type and constraints.
points: Commas separate definitions.
Every column needs a type.
Keep related columns together.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE demo (id INTEGER, title TEXT, active BOOLEAN, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());

topics.title: Creating Multiple Tables
topics.simple: Ek schema me alag-alag tables banao — students, courses, enrollments.
topics.pro: Create related tables in dependency order: parent tables first, then tables with foreign keys.
points: Create referenced tables before referencing tables.
Use consistent key types.
One statement per table is easier to review.

example.sql:
CREATE TABLE teachers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE rooms (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Table Schema
topics.simple: Schema table ka blueprint hai — columns, types, keys aur rules.
topics.pro: A table schema is its declared structure and constraints, distinct from the data it currently holds.
points: Schema changes are migrations.
Data changes are DML.
Inspect both structure and data separately.

example.sql: SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'students' ORDER BY ordinal_position;
example.output: One row per column with its type.

topics.title: CREATE SCHEMA and search_path
topics.simple: Schema database ke andar namespace hai; search_path batata hai unqualified naam kahan dhoondhna hai.
topics.pro: CREATE SCHEMA creates a namespace; search_path controls the order in which unqualified object names are resolved.
points: public is the default schema.
Qualify as school.students.
Put trusted schemas first in search_path.

example.sql:
CREATE SCHEMA school;
SET search_path TO school, public;

topics.title: CREATE TABLE AS
topics.simple: CREATE TABLE AS query ka result ek naye table me save karta hai.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE AS creates a table and fills it from a SELECT; it copies column names and data but not most constraints or indexes.
points: It is convenient for snapshots.
It does not copy primary keys automatically.
The command tag is SELECT N.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE top_students AS SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Creating Tables from Existing Data
topics.simple: Existing table ki structure ya data se naya table bana sakte hain.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE ... (LIKE source INCLUDING ALL) copies the structure; CREATE TABLE AS copies data; INSERT ... SELECT fills an existing table.
points: LIKE copies no rows.
CTAS copies rows but not constraints.
INSERT ... SELECT keeps the target definition.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students_copy (LIKE students INCLUDING ALL);

topics.title: IF NOT EXISTS
topics.simple: IF NOT EXISTS table already ho to error ke bajaye skip kar deta hai.
topics.pro: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS skips creation when the relation name already exists; it does not compare or migrate the existing definition.
points: Useful in repeatable bootstrap scripts.
Not a migration tool.
It emits a notice when skipping.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
example.output: CREATE TABLE (or NOTICE: relation already exists, skipping)

topics.title: Table Naming Conventions
topics.simple: Table ka naam plural, lowercase aur descriptive rakho — students, course_enrollments.
topics.pro: Use lower_snake_case, plural nouns and descriptive relationship names; avoid reserved words and quoted mixed case.
points: Be consistent across the schema.
Name join tables after both sides.
Keep names under 63 bytes.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_enrollments (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, enrolled_on DATE);

topics.title: Inspecting Table Structure
topics.simple: Table banne ke baad \d ya information_schema se structure check karo.
topics.pro: psql \d shows columns, types, indexes and constraints; information_schema.columns is the portable catalog query.
points: Inspect after every DDL change.
Check defaults and nullability.
Verify foreign keys explicitly.

example.sql: SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'courses';

topics.title: Common CREATE Errors
topics.simple: CREATE fail ho sakta hai duplicate table, missing type, duplicate column ya missing parent table se.
topics.pro: Common failures are relation already exists, column specified more than once, missing type, invalid default, missing referenced relation and permission denied.
points: Read the first error and the object name.
Use IF NOT EXISTS only when skipping is correct.
Create parent tables before foreign keys.

topics.title: CREATE TABLE with Foreign Keys
topics.simple: Foreign key child table ko parent table se jodta hai.
topics.pro: A foreign key references a candidate key in a parent table and enforces referential integrity; choose ON DELETE behaviour deliberately.
points: The parent key must be UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY.
ON DELETE CASCADE removes children.
Create the parent first.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Practical Student Database Design
topics.simple: Ab students, courses aur enrollments ka real schema banate hain.
topics.pro: A small school schema uses students, courses and a junction table with a composite primary key and foreign keys to both parents.
points: Every table has a primary key.
The junction table enforces one enrollment per pair.
Use consistent key types.

interview.q: What is the difference between a database and a schema?
interview.answer: A database is a separate catalog with its own connections; a schema is a namespace inside a database that groups objects.

interview.q: Why can CREATE DATABASE not run in a transaction?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL does not allow database creation inside a transaction block, so it cannot be rolled back like a table change.

interview.q: What is template1 vs template0?
interview.answer: template1 is the default template and may carry local customizations; template0 is pristine and is the safe base when changing encoding or locale.

interview.q: Who owns a newly created database?
interview.answer: The role that created it, unless OWNER is specified.

interview.q: Why does database encoding matter?
interview.answer: Encoding determines which characters can be stored and how text is represented; UTF8 is the usual choice for multilingual data.

interview.q: What are PostgreSQL identifier rules?
interview.answer: Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase, are limited to 63 bytes and must not be empty; reserved words need quoting.

interview.q: What does CREATE TABLE define?
interview.answer: Ordered columns, their data types, defaults and constraints, plus table-level constraints and storage options.

interview.q: What does a primary key guarantee?
interview.answer: Uniqueness and non-nullness for the key columns, backed by a unique index.

interview.q: Does a foreign key require a unique parent key?
interview.answer: Yes. The referenced columns must be a primary key or have a unique constraint.

interview.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
interview.answer: When the parent row is deleted, matching child rows are deleted automatically.

interview.q: What is the difference between SERIAL and IDENTITY?
interview.answer: SERIAL is a legacy pseudo-type that creates a sequence and default; GENERATED AS IDENTITY is standard SQL and preferred for new tables.

interview.q: What is the difference between CTAS and CREATE TABLE LIKE?
interview.answer: CTAS copies columns and rows from a query but not most constraints; LIKE copies the structure and can include constraints but no rows.

interview.q: Why is IF NOT EXISTS not a migration tool?
interview.answer: It only checks the relation name; it does not add missing columns or reconcile a different definition.

interview.q: What is search_path?
interview.answer: The ordered list of schemas PostgreSQL uses to resolve unqualified object names.

interview.q: How do you inspect a table in psql?
interview.answer: Use \d table for columns, indexes and constraints; \d+ adds storage and description details.

interview.q: What are common CREATE TABLE errors?
interview.answer: Relation already exists, duplicate column, missing type, invalid default, missing referenced table and permission denied.

interview.q: Why qualify table names with a schema?
interview.answer: Qualification removes ambiguity and protects against a hostile or unexpected search_path.

interview.q: What is a composite primary key?
interview.answer: A primary key made of two or more columns; the combination must be unique and none may be null.

interview.q: Does CTAS copy indexes?
interview.answer: No. CTAS creates a new table and data; indexes and most constraints must be added separately.

interview.q: What privilege is needed to create tables?
interview.answer: CREATE on the schema, plus USAGE on that schema; the role also needs a database connection.
